paragraphs: Suppose the State is a moral person whose life lies in the union of its members, and suppose the most important of its cares is its own preservation. Then it must have a universal and compelling force, to move and arrange each part in whatever way is most advantageous to the whole. Nature gives each man absolute power over all his members. In the same way, the social compact gives the body politic absolute power over all its members. And it is this power, when directed by the general will, that bears, as I have said, the name of Sovereignty.

But besides the public person, we have to consider the private persons who make it up, whose life and liberty are by nature independent of it. We must therefore distinguish clearly between the respective rights of the citizens and of the Sovereign,[1] and between the duties the citizens have to fulfill as subjects and the natural rights they should enjoy as men.

I admit that by the social compact each man gives away only that part of his powers, goods and liberty that it matters for the community to control. But it must also be granted that the Sovereign is the sole judge of what matters.

A citizen ought to perform every service he can for the State as soon as the Sovereign demands it. But the Sovereign, for its part, cannot impose on its subjects any fetters that are useless to the community, and cannot even wish to do so. For nothing can happen without a cause, whether by the law of reason or by the law of nature.

The undertakings that bind us to the social body are obligatory only because they are mutual. And their nature is such that in fulfilling them we cannot work for others without working for ourselves. Why is the general will always in the right, and why do all continually will the happiness of each one? Only because there is no one who does not think of “each” as meaning himself, and who does not consider himself when voting for all. This proves that equality of rights, and the idea of justice that such equality creates, originate in the preference each man gives to himself, and so in the very nature of man. It proves that the general will, to be really general, must be general in its object as well as its essence; that it must both come from all and apply to all; and that it loses its natural rectitude when it is directed at some particular and determinate object. For in that case we are judging something foreign to us, and have no true principle of equity to guide us.

Indeed, as soon as a question arises about a particular fact or right, on a point not previously regulated by a general convention, the matter becomes contentious. It is a case in which the individuals concerned are one party and the public the other, but in which I can see neither the law that ought to be followed nor the judge who ought to decide. It would be absurd in such a case to propose referring the question to an express decision of the general will. That decision can only be the conclusion reached by one of the parties, and so it will be, for the other party, merely an outside and particular will, inclined on this occasion to injustice and liable to error. Thus, just as a particular will cannot stand for the general will, the general will in turn changes its nature when its object is particular, and, being general, cannot pronounce on a man or a fact. For instance, when the people of Athens appointed or removed its rulers, decreed honors to one man and imposed penalties on another, and by a multitude of particular decrees exercised all the functions of government without distinction, it no longer had a general will in the strict sense. It was acting no longer as Sovereign, but as magistrate. This will seem contrary to current views, but I must be given time to set out my own.

It should be clear from the foregoing that what makes a will general is not so much the number of voters as the common interest that unites them. For under this system each necessarily submits to the conditions he imposes on others. This admirable agreement between interest and justice gives the common deliberations an equitable character. That character vanishes at once when any particular question is discussed, because there is no common interest to unite and identify the ruling of the judge with that of the party.

From whatever side we approach our principle, we reach the same conclusion: the social compact sets up among the citizens an equality of such a kind that they all bind themselves to observe the same conditions and should therefore all enjoy the same rights. Thus, from the very nature of the compact, every “act of Sovereignty,” _i.e._ every authentic act of the general will, binds or favors all the citizens equally. The Sovereign therefore recognizes only the body of the nation and makes no distinctions among those who compose it. What, then, strictly speaking, is an act of Sovereignty? It is not a convention between a superior and an inferior, but a convention between the body and each of its members. It is legitimate, because it is based on the social compact; equitable, because it is common to all; useful, because it can have no other object than the general good; and stable, because it is guaranteed by the public force and the supreme power. So long as the subjects have to submit only to conventions of this sort, they obey no one but their own will. And to ask how far the respective rights of the Sovereign and the citizens extend is to ask up to what point the citizens can enter into undertakings with themselves, each with all and all with each.

We can see from this that the sovereign power, absolute, sacred and inviolable as it is, does not and cannot exceed the limits of general conventions, and that every man may do as he likes with whatever goods and liberty these conventions leave him. So the Sovereign never has a right to lay more burdens on one subject than on another, because in that case the question becomes particular and is no longer within its competence.

Once these distinctions are admitted, it is clear how untrue it is that the individuals make any real renunciation in the social compact. The position they find themselves in as a result of the compact is actually better than the one they were in before. Instead of a renunciation, they have made an advantageous exchange. In place of an uncertain and precarious way of living, they have got one that is better and more secure. In place of natural independence, they have got liberty. In place of the power to harm others, they have got security for themselves. And in place of their strength, which others might overcome, they have got a right that social union makes invincible. Their very life, which they have devoted to the State, is constantly protected by it. And when they risk it in the State’s defense, what more are they doing than giving back what they have received from it? What are they doing that they would not do more often, and with greater danger, in the state of nature, where they would inevitably have to fight battles at the risk of their lives in defense of the very thing that is the means of their preservation? All have indeed to fight when their country needs them. But then no one ever has to fight for himself. Do we not gain something by running, on behalf of what gives us our security, only some of the risks we should have to run for ourselves as soon as we lost it?
